subtype: Approach: ask open questions to understand first [Action]
passage:
Family diary, written by Meena.

Sunday, 5 pm. Varun sat with my father Shankar on the veranda for almost an hour. I watched from the kitchen door. Instead of arguing about the new tax rules, Varun asked, "Nana, what made you feel so strongly about this?" My father spoke of the years he ran a cooperative shop, when prices jumped and the shelves emptied. Varun did not interrupt once; he only nodded and asked one more question.

At the end, Varun said calmly, "I see why it worries you. I think differently about one part, and here's why." My father raised an eyebrow, then laughed and said, "Well, at least you listened." I brought them tea and did not say a word.

qa.q: Where did Varun and Shankar talk?
qa.a: On the veranda, for almost an hour.

qa.q: What does Shankar's laugh at the end suggest he felt?
qa.a: Shankar likely felt heard and a little disarmed, as Varun's calm way of asking softened any defensiveness.

qa.q: What could Varun try in a later conversation to keep the talk open, and why?
qa.a: Varun could keep asking about Shankar's experiences and share a second view in the same calm tone, because curiosity keeps the door open even when opinions differ.

qa.q: How might Meena feel watching from the kitchen door?
qa.a: Meena may feel relieved and quietly proud, since the talk that might have been feared turned warm and was left uninterrupted.

grounding: The student asks the grandfather what shaped his view, listens without interrupting, then calmly shares one personal view.
